parts.partTitle: reduce vs collect & Map Collector Pitfalls

beats.headline: Using reduce to build a List makes your code O(n²).
beats.subline: Immutable folding creates a brand new list copy on every single element.
beats.narration: Using stream dot reduce to build a list creates a fresh array copy on every element, turning linear work into quadratic garbage collector torture. Let's see why collect is built completely differently.

beats.title: Immutable Fold vs. Mutable Accumulation

top.label: reduce(): Immutable Copy
points: Heavy GC pressure and slow execution

bottom.label: collect(): Mutable Container
points: Mutates a single container in place

beats.narration: Reduce folds immutable values like numbers. Passing a mutable list into reduce forces you to copy the entire collection on every element. Stream dot collect creates one container up front and mutates it in place.

beats.title: Collectors.toList vs Stream.toList()

steps.explanation: Returns a mutable list in OpenJDK, but has no strict mutability guarantee in specs. Permits null elements.
Java 16+ direct terminal operation. Returns an unmodifiable list and allows null elements.
Strictly unmodifiable and throws NullPointerException immediately if any element is null.

beats.narration: Collectors dot toList returns a mutable list and permits nulls. Java 16 introduced stream dot toList directly on the stream interface, returning an unmodifiable list while still allowing nulls. Use toUnmodifiableList to strictly forbid nulls.

beats.title: Collectors.toMap Duplicate Key Bug

steps.explanation: Throws IllegalStateException: Duplicate key if two stream items produce the exact same key value.
Resolves key collisions explicitly by merging existing and incoming values together.

beats.narration: The two-argument Collectors dot toMap throws an IllegalStateException the instant two elements share a key. Always pass a third argument merge function to handle collisions safely by keeping the existing, replacing with new, or combining values.

beats.title: Part 1 Locked In
takeaways: collect() is O(n) mutable accumulation; reduce() is immutable fold
Stream.toList() returns unmodifiable list; Collectors.toList() is mutable
Collectors.toMap requires a merge function to handle duplicate keys

beats.narration: That's the foundation of stream collection. In Part 2, we explore multi-level groupingBy, downstream collectors, and computing two aggregations in a single pass with teeing.

beats.headline: Filtering before groupingBy deletes empty groups completely.
beats.subline: Learn how downstream collectors preserve empty buckets and compute twin metrics in one pass.
beats.narration: Filtering your stream before calling groupingBy removes unmatched elements entirely, wiping out empty categories from your final map. Downstream collectors fix this problem and unleash powerful single-pass reports.

beats.title: How Downstream Collectors Work
beats.subtitle: Aggregating groups in a single pass without intermediate lists

nodes.label: Stream Elements
nodes.detail: Incoming record stream processed element by element

nodes.label: groupingBy Classifier
nodes.detail: Routes each element to a map bucket key

nodes.label: Downstream Collector
nodes.detail: Applies filtering, mapping, or summing inside the bucket

nodes.label: Final Map Result
nodes.detail: Map of domain keys to aggregated bucket results

beats.narration: GroupingBy routes incoming stream items to map keys based on a classifier function. Instead of producing intermediate lists, a downstream collector aggregates each bucket directly in place during the stream traversal.

beats.title: Multi-Level Grouping & Downstream Filtering

steps.explanation: Groups elements by customerId key. Classifier function must never return null.
Downstream filter preserves the key in the result map with an empty list if no transactions match.

beats.narration: Using Collectors dot filtering as a downstream collector keeps every customer key in the map, returning an empty list if no transactions match. Filtering before groupingBy would drop missing keys entirely from your final map.

beats.title: Twin Aggregations with Collectors.teeing

steps.explanation: Feeds every stream element into two independent collectors simultaneously.
Combines both partial results into a clean domain record when stream terminates.

beats.narration: Java 12 introduced Collectors dot teeing. It sends every stream element to two independent downstream collectors simultaneously, then merges their results into a domain record without traversing the stream twice.

beats.title: Part 2 Complete
takeaways: Collectors.filtering preserves empty keys in grouped maps
partitioningBy always guarantees true and false keys
Collectors.teeing computes two distinct metrics in a single pass

beats.narration: Now you can write complex single-pass groupings and twin aggregations. In Part 3, we build custom collectors with Collector dot of and avoid silent cast bugs.

beats.headline: Setting IDENTITY_FINISH on a custom collector can throw ClassCastException.
beats.subline: This optimization flag completely skips your finisher function!
beats.narration: Setting IDENTITY_FINISH on a custom collector tells the stream engine to bypass your finisher function entirely. If your finisher transforms or wraps your container, your app breaks with class cast exceptions.

beats.title: The 4 Contract Functions of Collector<T, A, R>
beats.subtitle: How stream engines build custom result containers

nodes.label: 1. supplier()
nodes.detail: Creates fresh mutable container A for each worker thread

nodes.label: 2. accumulator()
nodes.detail: Folds input item T into mutable container A

nodes.label: 3. combiner()
nodes.detail: Merges two partial containers during parallel execution

nodes.label: 4. finisher()
nodes.detail: Transforms intermediate container A into final result R

beats.narration: Every collector relies on four functions: supplier creates the mutable container, accumulator adds elements, combiner merges parallel chunks, and finisher transforms the container into your final result.

beats.title: Building a Batching Collector with Collector.of

steps.explanation: Creates a batch list and appends items into fixed-size inner chunk lists.
Wraps inner batches into unmodifiable lists. Skipped if IDENTITY_FINISH is set!

beats.narration: Here is a custom batching collector built with Collector dot of. It groups stream elements into fixed-size chunks. Because finisher wraps each batch into an unmodifiable list, we must omit the IDENTITY_FINISH characteristic.

beats.title: IDENTITY_FINISH Flag Behavior

top.label: IDENTITY_FINISH Included
points: Tells runtime intermediate A equals result R

bottom.label: Finisher Executes
points: Runs finisher function on final container
Safe for container wrappers and custom types

beats.narration: IDENTITY_FINISH promises that your intermediate container type and final result type are identical. If your finisher transforms the container to another type or wraps it, the engine skips finisher and causes runtime class cast errors.

beats.title: Part 3 Complete
takeaways: Custom collectors need supplier, accumulator, combiner, and finisher
Collector.of creates concise reusable collectors without custom classes
Never add IDENTITY_FINISH if finisher performs a transformation

parts.partTitle: Parallel Streams, Fork/Join Pool & Production Traps

beats.headline: Adding parallelStream to HTTP calls can stall your whole JVM.
beats.subline: The shared ForkJoinPool.commonPool has very few worker threads.
beats.narration: Calling parallelStream on blocking HTTP or database queries is a dangerous production trap. It runs on the JVM shared Fork Join common pool, parking all worker threads and stalling unrelated tasks across your service.

beats.title: Fork/Join Work-Stealing Pool Mechanics
beats.subtitle: How parallel streams split spliterators across CPU cores

nodes.label: Spliterator Split
nodes.detail: Splits source data array into balanced work chunks

nodes.label: Worker Thread Deques
nodes.detail: Each pool thread processes tasks from its local queue

nodes.label: Work Stealing
nodes.detail: Idle threads steal tasks from busy thread deque tails

nodes.label: Combiner Merge
nodes.detail: Combines thread partial results into single final output

beats.narration: Parallel streams use Spliterators to decompose data. Workers store subtasks in local deques and steal work from busy threads when idle. Finally, combiner functions merge partial accumulators into the final output.

beats.title: Benchmarking Parallel Stream Sources
beats.caption: Spliterator performance varies wildly by data structure

lines.text: # Array & IntStream split in O(1) time - High Speed
Benchmark                        Mode  Cnt   Score   Error  Units
# LinkedList & iterate split in O(n) - Slow & Overhead

beats.narration: Data structures with fixed indexed layout like arrays and IntStream split in O(1) time, giving massive parallel speedups. LinkedList and stream dot iterate split in linear time, adding thread coordination overhead that makes code slower.

beats.title: groupingByConcurrent for Unordered Parallel Streams

steps.explanation: Creates partial HashMaps on each thread, then merges them sequentially in combiner().
Uses a single ConcurrentHashMap directly, skipping costly map merge operations entirely.

beats.narration: When grouping unordered data on parallel streams, standard groupingBy creates separate maps per thread and merges them. Switching to groupingByConcurrent uses a single shared ConcurrentHashMap, bypassing combiner merge overhead completely.

beats.title: Chapter Complete! Run the Lab
takeaways: Parallel streams run on the shared JVM ForkJoinPool.commonPool
Avoid parallel streams for blocking I/O; use for heavy CPU tasks
Use groupingByConcurrent to avoid map merge costs on parallel streams
